summary:
Minas Gerais is a state within Brazil and stands under the national framework set out for that country: same-sex marriage legal nationwide since 2013, the Supreme Federal Tribunal's 2018 removal of the surgical requirement for legal gender change, an equal age of consent regardless of sexual orientation, and, since the Supreme Court's 2019 ruling, constitutional and federal criminal provisions under which discrimination and hate crimes on sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds are punished and transphobia is treated on the same footing as racism. An expat legal guide updated in April 2026 confirms that same-sex marriage, spousal-visa equality and gender-marker rules operate nationwide, so a trans visitor's documents and family-law status are handled the same as anyone else's at entry.

The dominant visitor-facing risk in Minas Gerais is lethal violence against trans people, and the state sits at the severe end of the national picture. The ANTRA dossier for 2024, published 27 January 2025, ranks Minas Gerais second nationally with 12 trans killings during the year, behind São Paulo with 16 and ahead of Ceará with 11. The cumulative count for the state across 2017 to 2024 is 100.

The following year's figures put the state at the head of the national ranking. The ANTRA dossier for 2025, reported on 26 January 2026, records Minas Gerais tied with Ceará in first place with 8 trans killings during 2025, within a national total of 80.

Detention in the state operates under a defined federal rule-set. A portaria issued on 17 April 2014 by the Secretaria de Direitos Humanos da Presidência da República sets housing rules for LGBT prisoners across Brazil's prison system and applies within the Minas Gerais state prison system. Transsexual men and women must be forwarded to female prison units, gay and travesti prisoners held in male prisons must be offered specific conviviality spaces, and LGBT inmates may use their social name, which must appear in the admission record, together with the choice of male or female clothing.
tangentialFactors:
Minas Gerais is measured against other Brazilian states in the same reporting cycles rather than in isolation. In 2024 it stood behind São Paulo and ahead of Ceará; in 2025 it was level with Ceará at the top of the national ranking. Its own count fell from 12 killings to 8 across the two years while its relative position rose.

The gap between the statutory position and lived experience is a national feature that reaches the state. Outright International's country overview, updated in March 2026, records that LGBTIQ people in Brazil still face significant violence and discrimination despite the constitutional and criminal provisions. In the October 2024 municipal elections close to 1,000 transgender candidates stood across every state of the country and received death threats and intimidation, while the number of trans officeholders tripled compared with the previous cycle.

Courts have read the protective provisions into commercial conduct: the 27th Private Chamber of the São Paulo Court of Justice upheld a moral-damage award against a nightclub that refused entry to a trans woman wearing women's clothing, affirming the compensation ordered at first instance in Barra Bonita. Lower courts have also pressed the Superior Court of Justice toward extending the remedies of the Maria da Penha Law and the Feminicide Law to trans women, per an analysis of case law from 2022.
localsOnly:
The 2014 portaria governs the state prison system as residents experience it. Transsexual men and women are to be forwarded to female prison units; gay and travesti prisoners held in male prisons are to be offered specific conviviality spaces; and LGBT inmates may use their social name, which must appear in the admission record, and may choose male or female clothing.

That instrument provides no sanctions for non-compliance. Residents therefore have a stated entitlement on paper without a penalty attached to its breach, and the source reporting the portaria documents no Minas Gerais-specific implementation, wing, segregation practice or case.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the Minas Gerais state prison system operates a designated LGBTI wing, or applies the 2014 portaria in practice, is unresolved: the sources in this record document no state-specific implementation, segregation practice or case, and none reports a complaint or judicial finding on the point.

The killing figures are tallies published by ANTRA and reported through news outlets; this record contains no official state or federal homicide breakdown for Minas Gerais against which those counts can be checked, and no breakdown by motive or by whether the victim was a visitor.

Nothing in this record addresses bathroom or facility access, access to healthcare, hate-crime prosecutions or police conduct in Minas Gerais specifically. Those are not sourced here rather than cleared.
